summary.text: The El Niño–Southern Oscillation is a global climate phenomenon in which sea surface temperatures over the tropical Pacific swing between a warm phase, El Niño, and a cool phase, La Niña.
The switches between El Niño, La Niña and neutral conditions are irregular, coming roughly every two to seven years, and they bring intense storms to some places and droughts to others.
At its heart is a feedback between wind and sea: weaker trade winds let warm water surge east, which warms the sea surface and weakens the winds even more.

facts.label: Cycle length
facts.value: Roughly every two to seven years

facts.label: Name origin
facts.value: Spanish for "The Boy", after the Christ Child

facts.label: Global temperature
facts.value: El Niño spikes it for about a year

facts.label: Pacific sea level
facts.value: About 0.5 m higher near Indonesia than Peru

items.prompt: The sea off Peru sits in the tropics, yet it is usually much cooler than the western Pacific. What keeps it cool?

options.label: Cold deep water rising up, plus a current from the far south
Meltwater from Andes glaciers pouring into the coastal sea
Thick cloud cover that blocks most incoming sunlight
Icy winds blowing steadily down from the North Pole

items.explain: Deep cold water upwells to replace surface water pushed away, and the Humboldt Current brings cold water north from the Southern Ocean.

items.prompt: Peruvian fishermen named a warm coastal current after the newborn Christ. Why that name?

options.label: It was first noticed by a young boy on a fishing boat
It was weak and small compared with other currents
It usually showed up around the Christmas season
It was thought to bless the fishing with bigger catches

items.explain: The warm current typically appeared around Christmas, so it was named after the Christ Child: El Niño, "The Boy".

items.prompt: The easterly trade winds along the equatorial Pacific slacken for several weeks. What follows?

options.label: Cold water upwells more strongly along the equator
Warm surface water surges east and the sea there warms
Warm water piles up even higher in the far west
The eastern Pacific cools into a La Niña phase

items.explain: Weaker trade winds send warm surface water east and cut upwelling, warming the sea and weakening the winds further.

items.prompt: Strong trade winds keep pushing warm surface water westward across the equatorial Pacific. Where would you expect the sea surface to stand higher?

options.label: Off Peru, on the eastern side of the ocean
Nowhere; sea level stays flat across the ocean
In the middle of the ocean, far from both coasts
Near Indonesia, on the western side of the ocean

items.explain: Water driven west by the winds builds up, so sea level near Indonesia is typically about half a metre higher than near Peru.

items.prompt: Which kind of country tends to be hit hardest when ENSO swings between its phases?

options.label: Wealthy industrial nations in northern Europe
Landlocked desert countries in central Asia
Small island nations scattered in the Arctic
Developing Pacific nations that rely on farms and fishing

items.explain: The countries most affected are developing countries on the Pacific that depend on agriculture and fishing.

items.prompt: Over one decade, El Niño events happen much more often than La Niña events. What does that do to the global temperature trend for that decade?

options.label: It pulls the trend toward cooling
It tilts the trend toward warming
It has no effect on the trend
It only changes ocean, not air, warmth

items.explain: Each El Niño briefly spikes global surface temperature, so a run of them nudges the ten-year trend warmer.

pack.title: When the Trade Winds Falter
pack.question: Why does the tropical Pacific flip between warm and cool years?

hero.credit: Content published by Rebecca Lindsey and reviewed by Tom Di Liberto. Image credi · Public domain

beats.title: When the Trade Winds Falter
beats.hook: A slackening of the winds over the Pacific can end in intense storms in some places and droughts in others.

beats.prompt: The easterly trade winds over the equatorial Pacific weaken. What happens next in the eastern Pacific?
beats.explain: Weaker trade winds send warm surface water east and reduce upwelling, which warms the sea, weakens the Walker circulation and weakens the winds still more.

choices.label: Cold upwelling grows stronger and the sea there cools
choices.feedback: Upwelling actually drops when the winds weaken, because less surface water is pushed away.

choices.label: Warm water stays piled up in the west
choices.feedback: The winds were what held warm water in the west; when they weaken it surges east.

choices.label: Warm water surges east, the sea warms and the winds weaken further
The winds bounce back at once and nothing changes
choices.feedback: The change feeds on itself: warmer water weakens the winds even more.

beats.prompt: Put the steps of an El Niño in order.

items.label: The sea warms and the winds weaken even more
Warm water in the west runs low and conditions return to normal

beats.explain: Weaker winds move warm water east, the warming weakens the winds further, until the western store of warm water is used up.

beats.prompt: Match each term to what it means.

right.label: Cold deep water rising to the surface
The cooling phase of Pacific sea temperatures
The swing in air pressure across the tropical Pacific
The warming phase of Pacific sea temperatures

beats.explain: ENSO couples an ocean swing (El Niño and La Niña) with an air pressure swing, and upwelling is what normally keeps the east cool.

beats.prompt: In normal years, sort each feature to the side of the tropical Pacific where it is found.
beats.explain: Trade winds pile warm water in the west, deepening the warm layer there, while cold water wells up in the east.

beats.idea: Winds and sea temperatures push on each other, so weaker trade winds can grow into an El Niño that disrupts weather around the world.
